title: The kitchen behind your Python

beats.say: You write Python, so why does your Spark job crash with a Java error?

show.sub: Something else is running your job

beats.say: Picture a restaurant. Your Python code is the waiter. The kitchen is the Java Virtual Machine, a program that runs Java and Scala code. The waiter takes orders. The kitchen cooks.
Spark, Flink, Kafka and Trino all have their kitchens inside the JVM. So when something burns, the complaint comes back in Java words.

show.title: Kitchens that run on the JVM

beats.say: A slow job often means the waiter carries one plate at a time. Let the kitchen do the work itself, and service speeds up.

show.text: Let the kitchen do the work

check.q: In the restaurant picture, why does a Spark job written in Python show Java errors?
opts: Python is secretly converted into Java text files
The real work happens in the JVM, so errors come from there
Spark only works if you also write Java
check.why: Your Python is just the front end. The JVM does the actual cooking, so failures surface in JVM terms.

work: Open a failed Spark job log and find the first line that mentions a Java exception.
List which tools in your stack run on the JVM.

title: From PySpark call to executor

beats.say: What really happens when you call filter on a PySpark dataframe?
Your Python talks over a bridge called Py4J to the Spark driver, a JVM process. The driver builds a plan and hands tasks to executors, which are JVMs on many machines.
A built in function, like upper, runs entirely inside those executors. No Python process is ever started.

A Python UDF, a function you write yourself, is different. Every row is serialised, sent to a Python worker, processed, and sent back. A hundred million rows means a hundred million round trips. A pandas UDF ships whole batches in Arrow format, so the trips drop to thousands.

check.q: Why is a pandas UDF usually faster than a plain Python UDF?
opts: It runs inside the JVM
It moves whole Arrow batches instead of one row at a time
It skips the Spark driver
check.why: Both leave the JVM, but batches in Arrow format cut the number of crossings and the serialisation cost per row.

work: Find every Python UDF in your jobs and check whether a built in function can replace it.
Compare run time of one UDF versus its pandas UDF version on the same data.

title: Heap, GC pauses and silent kills

beats.say: Your executor died of out of memory, yet the machine had gigabytes free. How?

show.sub: The JVM has its own limits

beats.say: The JVM only uses a fixed heap, set by executor memory. Say eight gigabytes. Python workers and buffers live outside it, in overhead. If the total passes the container limit, Kubernetes or YARN kills it.

The second trap is garbage collection. The JVM frees memory by pausing your code to sweep up dead objects. On a huge heap, one pause can last seconds. Heartbeats are missed, and a healthy executor looks dead.
Check GC time in the Spark UI. Over ten percent of task time is a warning. Fix it with more partitions, smaller tasks, no collect on big data, and more memory overhead when using Python UDFs.

show.title: Fixes to try
items: GC time under ten percent of task time
Raise memory overhead for Python UDFs

check.q: An executor is killed by the cluster although the JVM heap was not full. What is the likely cause?
opts: Heap plus off-heap overhead exceeded the container limit
The driver ran a garbage collection
Py4J closed the connection
check.why: Python workers and buffers sit outside the heap. The container limit covers heap plus overhead, so the total can exceed it.

work: Check GC time per task in the Spark UI for your slowest job.
Set memory overhead explicitly for any job that uses Python UDFs.

title: Python or Scala: the trade-off

beats.say: Should your team rewrite Python Spark jobs in Scala to make them faster?
Usually no. Dataframe code in Python builds the same plan as Scala, and the JVM runs it at the same speed. A rewrite buys nothing there.
Scala pays off only for custom row by row logic. A Python UDF crosses the process boundary for every row. A Scala UDF stays inside the JVM.
But the cost is real. Scala engineers are scarcer, onboarding is slower, and your machine learning libraries live in Python.
So choose in order: built in functions, then pandas UDF, then a Scala jar for the proven hot path. Measure before you move.

check.q: A Python dataframe job is slow, and profiling shows a Python UDF applied to every row. What is the best first step?
opts: Rewrite the whole job in Scala
Replace it with built in functions or a pandas UDF
Add more driver memory
check.why: The cost is the per row crossing into Python. Built ins or batch based pandas UDFs remove most of it without a language rewrite.

work: Write a team rule: built ins first, pandas UDF second, Scala only with benchmark proof.
Profile one slow job and record how much time goes to Python UDFs.

title: Scala is Python in permanent marker

beats.say: Why does Scala feel so strict when you come from Python? Think of it as writing in permanent marker instead of pencil.

In Python, a name is pencil. You can rub it out and write something else. In Scala, val is marker. Once you write val x equals five, x stays five. Nobody can change it behind your back while your job runs on fifty machines.

Missing values work like a lunchbox. Python might hand you nothing and let you bite into air. Scala gives you an Option box. It is either Some with food inside, or None, which is empty. The compiler makes you open it and check before eating.

check.q: What does Option[Int] force you to do?
opts: Handle both a value and a missing value
Convert the number to text
Run the code twice
Reassign the variable
check.why: Option is either Some with a value or None, and the compiler makes you deal with both cases, so missing data cannot slip through silently.

work: Find one Python function in your code that can return None and write down how its callers handle it.
Prefer val over var in every Scala snippet you write this week.

title: Python to Scala, line by line

beats.say: How do you turn a Python list comprehension into Scala? You chain steps instead of nesting them.

show.title: Comprehension to chain
show.text:
[f(x) for x in xs if p(x)]
xs.filter(p).map(f)

beats.say: Filter keeps the items that pass a test. Map changes each one. Types go after names, so def add a colon Int, b colon Int, colon Int equals a plus b. The last expression is returned, so there is no return keyword. A lambda t arrow t dot fare shortens to underscore dot fare.

show.title: Functions
show.text:
def add(a: Int, b: Int): Int = a + b
trips.map(_.fare)

beats.say: A case class, like Trip with an id Long and a fare Double, gives you equality, copy and pattern matching for free. And foldLeft zero point zero, with underscore plus underscore dot fare, adds up all the fares starting from zero.

show.title: Case class and fold
show.text:
case class Trip(id: Long, fare: Double)
trips.foldLeft(0.0)(_ + _.fare)

check.q: What does xs.filter(p).map(f) do?
opts: Applies f to all items, then filters
Keeps items where p is true, then applies f to each
Sums the items using f
Mutates xs in place
check.why: Filter runs first and keeps only items that pass p. Map then transforms each survivor. The original collection is immutable and unchanged.

work: Rewrite three Python comprehensions from your codebase as filter and map chains.
Convert one dataclass to a case class and note what you get for free.

title: Encoders, Option.get and version traps

beats.say: Your Spark job compiles, then fails with unable to find encoder. What happened?

Spark needs an encoder to turn your case class into its compact binary row format. Scala passes it in automatically through implicits, but only when it is in scope. Add import spark.implicits._ and the error goes. The same import enables the dollar col syntax and toDS.

Another trap is calling get on an Option. On None it throws, so you lose the safety. Use match, map, or getOrElse instead. And a jar built for Scala 2.12 can crash on a 2.13 Spark cluster with NoSuchMethodError, so match the versions.

show.title: Gotchas
items: Check the build version before spark-submit

check.q: A jar built with Scala 2.12 fails on a cluster with NoSuchMethodError. Most likely cause?
opts: Missing val keyword
Scala binary version mismatch with the cluster's Spark
Too many case classes
Option used instead of null
check.why: Scala versions are not binary compatible across 2.12 and 2.13, so compiled calls point to methods that do not exist at runtime.

work: Check the Scala version of your Spark cluster and set the same one in build.sbt.
Search your code for .get on Options and replace each with getOrElse or match.

title: Scala or Python for Spark jobs?

beats.say: Should your team write Spark jobs in Scala or Python?

For plain DataFrame code it barely matters. Both build the same plan and Spark runs it on the JVM. Python only hurts with row by row UDFs, because every row crosses from the JVM to a Python process and back. Scala UDFs stay inside the JVM.

Scala has costs too. Fewer people know it. Builds need sbt and jar packaging, and you must pin Spark's Scala version. Typed Dataset lambdas also hide logic from the optimizer, so they can be slower than column expressions.

show.title: Scala costs
items: Typed lambdas are opaque to the optimizer

beats.say: So choose Python for most pipelines, using built-in functions. Choose Scala for heavy custom logic, shared libraries, or platform code that touches Spark internals.

show.title: Decision
items: Scala: shared libraries and platform code

check.q: When does PySpark most clearly lose to Scala?
opts: Simple DataFrame select and join
Row by row Python UDFs on huge data
Reading Parquet files
Writing to a table
check.why: Built-in DataFrame operations run in the JVM either way. Python UDFs move every row between the JVM and a Python process, which is costly at scale.

work: Audit your PySpark jobs for Python UDFs and swap in built-in functions where possible.
Write down your team's Scala skill level before approving a Scala-only platform library.

title: Kubernetes as a shared kitchen

beats.say: What if a hundred cooks shared one giant kitchen, and nobody ever fought over a stove?
That kitchen is Kubernetes. It runs your programs, packed in sealed boxes called containers, across many computers. A pod is one box, or a few that travel together, like one Spark worker.
Each team gets its own counter, called a namespace, with a limit on how much it may use. A job is a cook who finishes one dish and leaves. A deployment is a cook who stays all day.

show.title: Who does what
items: Namespace: a team's counter, with a cap

beats.say: When the kitchen is full, a priority label lets an urgent order bump a casual one. You just describe what you need, and the manager finds the space.

check.q: In the kitchen analogy, what is a namespace?
opts: A cook who stays all day
A team's own counter with a usage cap
The manager who assigns work
check.why: A namespace is a team's slice of the cluster, and a ResourceQuota caps how much that slice can use.

work: List the namespaces your team can use and find the quota on yours.
Name one job in your stack that is a run-once Job and one that is a long-running Deployment.

title: What happens when Spark meets Kubernetes

beats.say: When you submit a Spark job to Kubernetes, who actually creates the workers?
Submit asks the cluster's API server for one pod, the driver. The driver then asks the same API server for, say, twenty executor pods. Each pod states a request: the memory and CPU it needs reserved.
The scheduler only places a pod on a machine with that much room free. If none has room, the pod sits Pending, and describe shows Insufficient memory.
With the Spark Operator, you write a short SparkApplication spec instead. The operator runs the submit for you, restarts failures, and cleans up afterward.

show.sub: a short spec; the operator does the rest

check.q: A Spark executor pod stays Pending. What is the most likely cause?
opts: No node has enough free memory or CPU for its request
The shuffle files were lost
The driver heap is too large
check.why: The scheduler reserves requests; if no node can fit them, the pod waits Pending with an Insufficient message.

work: Read one SparkApplication spec and find the driver and executor requests.
Compare total executor requests with your namespace quota.

title: Why executors die with OOMKilled

beats.say: Your Spark job runs fine on a laptop, then pods keep dying with OOMKilled. Why?

show.sub: pods die, Spark shows no error

beats.say: A pod has a memory limit, a hard ceiling. Go over it and Linux kills the container at once. Spark gets no chance to log an error, you just see a dead pod.
The trap is that heap is not Spark's only memory. Python workers, network buffers and off-heap data live outside it. That extra is called memory overhead.
So the limit must cover heap plus overhead. With eight gigabytes of heap and two of overhead, the pod needs ten. Set memoryOverhead explicitly, and confirm with describe pod.

check.q: Executors have an 8 GB heap and the pod limit is exactly 8 GB. What is likely?
opts: Fine, heap is all Spark uses
OOMKilled, because overhead memory has no room
Pods will stay Pending forever
check.why: Non-heap memory counts toward the pod limit, so the limit must be heap plus overhead.

work: Set spark.executor.memoryOverhead explicitly instead of trusting the default.
Run kubectl describe pod on a dead executor and look for OOMKilled.

title: Why a lost pod can cost you a stage

beats.say: One executor pod dies mid-job. Why can that force Spark to redo work?
In a shuffle, each executor writes intermediate files to its local disk, and other executors fetch them. A pod's disk vanishes when the pod does.
Spark must recompute those files. Worse, dynamic allocation shrinks idle executors, which could delete files other tasks still need.
Two fixes. Shuffle tracking keeps an idle executor alive until its files are no longer needed. Or a remote shuffle service holds the files outside the pods, so they survive.

check.q: Why does dynamic allocation need shuffle tracking on Kubernetes?
opts: To speed up pod scheduling
To avoid removing executors whose shuffle files are still needed
To raise the memory limit
check.why: Pods are disposable, so removing an idle executor also removes its shuffle files unless tracked or stored remotely.

work: Check whether your jobs enable shuffle tracking when dynamic allocation is on.
Find which stages recompute after an executor loss in the Spark UI.

title: Reading cluster state fast

beats.say: A pod is stuck and someone asks why. Where do you look first?
Kubectl get pods with dash n team finance lists pods in that namespace and their state: Running, Pending or Error.
Describe pod tells the story. Pending with Insufficient memory means no node has room. Last state OOMKilled means it hit its limit.
Logs shows what the program printed before dying. Top pod shows live memory use, so you can compare it with the limit.

check.q: Which command shows that a pod was OOMKilled?
opts: kubectl logs
kubectl describe pod
kubectl get namespaces
check.why: Describe shows the pod's last state and events, including OOMKilled and scheduling failures.

work: Practice the four commands on a failing test pod.
Add a describe step to your on-call runbook.

title: Spot nodes for cheap batch compute

beats.say: How do you cut a batch compute bill by sixty to eighty percent?
Run executors on spot nodes, spare cloud machines sold at a discount that the provider can take back with short notice.
It works when losing an executor is cheap. Keep the driver on a regular node, since losing it kills the job. Add a remote shuffle service so reclaimed executors do not force recomputation.
Avoid spot for Flink jobs with big state or tight latency. They need stable nodes, plus checkpoints in object storage so a restarted TaskManager resumes.

check.q: Which placement is the best fit for spot nodes?
opts: The Spark driver
Spark executors with remote shuffle
A Flink job with large state and strict latency
check.why: Executors are disposable if their shuffle files survive; the driver and large stateful streaming jobs are costly to lose.

work: Put drivers on on-demand nodes and executors on spot with node selectors.
Measure rerun cost after a spot reclaim before committing.

title: When Kubernetes is the wrong choice

beats.say: Is Kubernetes always the right home for data jobs? No, and the trade-offs matter.
You gain one platform, team quotas, and priority classes so critical jobs pre-empt ad hoc ones when the cluster fills. Operators like Spark, Flink and Strimzi automate the routine work.
You pay in complexity. Memory limits, lost shuffle files and noisy neighbours become your problem. A small team with a few nightly jobs may be better off on a managed Spark service.
Choose Kubernetes when many teams share capacity and you want cost control. Choose managed services when your team is small and operations time is scarcer than money.

check.q: Which situation favors a managed Spark service over Kubernetes?
opts: Twenty teams sharing one large pool
A small team with a few nightly jobs and no platform staff
A need for priority pre-emption across teams
check.why: Kubernetes pays off through sharing and control; a small team may not recover the operational cost.

work: Estimate the engineer time your team spends on cluster operations.
Define a PriorityClass policy before the cluster gets crowded.

title: Typed or untyped: safety versus speed

beats.say: Would you rather have a spell checker, or a speed coach? In Spark's Scala API, you sometimes have to choose.

show.sub: Two ways to write the same filter

beats.say: Think of a typed Dataset as a form with named boxes. Fare must be a number. If you write the wrong thing, the compiler, which is the program that checks your code before it runs, stops you at once.
But the typed way hides your rule inside a little function. Spark's planner, called Catalyst, cannot read inside it. It is like a sealed envelope: the warehouse cannot sort it early.
A column expression is an open note. Catalyst reads it and skips unwanted rows early. So use typed for safety, and open notes for heavy work.

show.title: Pick by the job
items: Typed Dataset: safety at the edges

check.q: Why can Spark's planner not optimise a typed Scala lambda filter?
opts: Lambdas are too slow to run
The lambda is compiled code it cannot read inside
Typed Datasets cannot hold numbers
The compiler removes the filter
check.why: Catalyst optimises expressions it can inspect. A lambda is opaque compiled code, like a sealed envelope, so Catalyst cannot push it down.

work: Find one typed filter in your Spark code and ask whether a column expression would do.
Name where in your pipeline safety matters most, such as reading input.

title: Pushdown: one filter, two costs

beats.say: A trips table holds one billion rows, and you want fares over one hundred. Why does the way you write that filter change the runtime?

Write dollar fare greater than one hundred, and Spark gets an expression it understands. Catalyst pushes it into the Parquet scan, so files and row groups whose maximum fare is under one hundred are never read.
Write underscore dot fare greater than one hundred on a Dataset of Trip, and Spark gets compiled Scala bytecode. It must build a Trip object for every row, then run your function. Nothing is skipped.
Same result, very different work. One reads a slice of the files. The other reads all one billion rows.

check.q: You filter a Dataset of Trip with a typed lambda. What does Spark do that it would avoid with a column expression?
opts: Pushes the filter into the Parquet scan
Skips files by their maximum value
Builds a Trip object for every row and runs your function
Reads only the fare column
check.why: A lambda cannot be pushed down, so Spark reads the rows, builds Trip objects, and calls the function on each one.

work: Run explain on a typed filter and a column filter and compare PushedFilters.
Rewrite one hot typed filter as a column expression and time it.

title: Scala versus PySpark syntax traps

beats.say: Why does a PySpark filter with and sometimes crash, while the Scala one just works?
In Scala, equals is three equals signs, and not equals is equals bang equals. Those are Column methods that build an expression, not plain comparisons. Double ampersand and double pipe mean and, or.
PySpark uses single ampersand and single pipe. Python's operator precedence binds them tighter than comparisons, so each side needs brackets, or you get an error.
Naming a column uses the as method in Scala, and the alias method in Python. And isNotNull needs empty brackets in Python, but not in Scala.

check.q: Why does a PySpark filter like F.col("a") > 1 & F.col("b") < 5 fail?
opts: Python has no and operator
Ampersand binds tighter than greater-than, so each side needs brackets
Columns cannot be compared to numbers
It must use double ampersand
check.why: Python's & binds tighter than comparisons, so without brackets it combines 1 and the column first and errors.

work: Add brackets around every side of combined PySpark conditions.
When porting code, translate three equals to double equals and equals bang equals to bang equals.

title: What an opaque lambda really costs

beats.say: What actually happens when Spark meets a Scala lambda it cannot read?

Catalyst plans with expression trees. A lambda is just opaque compiled code, so there is no tree to inspect. Spark must decode each row's binary format into a Trip object, call your function, and read the result.
That has three costs. No pushdown into the scan. Extra garbage as millions of short-lived objects fill the JVM heap. And it breaks Spark's fused code generation around that step.

show.title: Three costs
items: Garbage: short-lived objects on the heap

beats.say: To check, run explain and look at PushedFilters. If it is empty when you expected your fare rule, a lambda is the likely cause.

check.q: In explain output, PushedFilters is empty for your fare rule. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The table is too small
The filter is a typed lambda Catalyst cannot inspect
Parquet does not support numbers
Spark cached the result
check.why: Only expressions Catalyst can read are pushed to the source. A typed lambda is opaque, so the list stays empty.

work: Make explain a routine check on slow jobs and look at PushedFilters.
Search the codebase for filter and map with underscore lambdas on big tables.

title: Where typed Datasets belong

beats.say: Should your platform use typed Datasets everywhere, or never?
Neither. Use typed Datasets at the edges: reading input, defining domain objects, and unit tests, where a compile error beats a midnight failure when a column is renamed.
Use untyped DataFrames for heavy joins, filters and aggregations over big tables, because pushdown and column pruning can cut scanned data sharply.
If your team writes PySpark, Scala's edge shrinks to typed APIs and custom code on the JVM. Pick Scala for that, not for speed of ordinary DataFrame work, which is the same in both.

check.q: Which design best balances safety and performance on a large platform?
opts: Typed lambdas for every transformation
Untyped everywhere, with no tests
Typed Datasets at the edges, DataFrame column expressions for heavy transformations
Switch to Scala purely for faster DataFrames
check.why: Typed edges catch schema mistakes cheaply, while column expressions let Catalyst optimise the heavy middle. Ordinary DataFrame speed is the same in Scala and PySpark.

work: Define case classes for your source and sink tables, and convert to DataFrame in the middle.
Add a review rule: typed lambdas on large tables need an explain check.
Decide Scala versus PySpark by need for typed APIs or JVM code, not by speed.

title: Hadoop as a giant library

beats.say: Why do so many big companies still run a cluster design from over ten years ago?

show.sub: Many large employers run it next to the cloud

beats.say: Picture a huge library. HDFS is the shelves. Every book is cut into chunks, and three copies of each chunk sit in different rooms, so one flooded room loses nothing. The head librarian, called the NameNode, keeps the index of where every chunk lives.
YARN is the desk manager. It hands out reading desks, called containers, to jobs that need memory and space. Hive is the card catalogue that lets you ask questions in plain SQL.

chip.text: Many firms are moving this to the cloud

check.q: In the library picture, what does the NameNode do?
opts: Stores every chunk itself
Keeps the index of where each chunk lives
Hands out reading desks to jobs
check.why: The NameNode holds metadata only: which chunks exist and where. The data sits on data nodes, and YARN hands out the desks.

work: Find out which of your company's pipelines still run on Hadoop.
Ask who owns the NameNode and the Hive catalogue today.

title: HDFS blocks and YARN containers

beats.say: How does a one terabyte file survive when a disk dies?

HDFS cuts the file into 128 megabyte blocks, about eight thousand of them. Each block is copied to three data nodes. The NameNode keeps the block map in memory. When a node dies, the NameNode notices and re-copies the missing blocks.

Now compute. Spark asks the YARN ResourceManager for executors. It hands out containers, say eight gigabytes and two vcores, on worker machines. The scheduler prefers machines that already hold the blocks, which is data locality, so less data crosses the network.

chip.text: Compute runs next to the data

check.q: A node holding some blocks dies. What keeps the data safe?
opts: The NameNode re-copies blocks from the surviving replicas
YARN restarts the file
Spark rebuilds the blocks from the query
check.why: Each block has three replicas. The NameNode sees the lost copies and orders new ones from the surviving nodes.

work: Work out how many blocks your largest table uses at 128 MB each.
List the container sizes your Spark jobs request.

title: Hive metastore and partitions

beats.say: When you run select from sales, how does the engine know which files to read?

It asks the Hive metastore. That is a database of table names, columns and partitions. Spark, Trino and Impala all read the same one. A partition is just a directory, like sales slash date equals 2026-01-05.

For one day, the engine lists that directory and reads only those files. But with years of partitions, listing gets slow. And if two writers touch a directory at once, readers can see half-written data. Iceberg fixes this by tracking files in metadata with snapshots.

show.title: Where Hive partitions hurt
items: Listing directories at query time is slow
No safe commits for concurrent writers
Iceberg tracks files and snapshots in metadata

check.q: Why is Hive's directory-based partitioning unsafe for concurrent writers?
opts: Partitions are stored in memory
Readers can see half-written files because there is no atomic snapshot
The metastore only allows one engine
check.why: Directories have no atomic commit, so readers may see partial output. Iceberg snapshots make a commit all-or-nothing.

work: Count the partitions in your biggest Hive table.
Time a partition listing on that table to see the cost.

title: Small files and killed containers

beats.say: Why can ten million tiny files bring down a petabyte cluster that is mostly empty?

show.text: Disk is free. Cluster is down.

beats.say: Every file and every block is an object in the NameNode's memory. Millions of tiny files use up that memory long before the disks fill, and each file also spawns its own slow task. The fix is compaction: merge them into files near 128 megabytes.

Second gotcha. YARN kills an executor container when heap plus memoryOverhead goes over the container size. Off-heap buffers and Python workers live in that overhead. Raise memoryOverhead, don't just grow the heap. It is the YARN twin of Kubernetes OOMKilled.

check.q: A Spark executor on YARN is killed though its heap never overflowed. Most likely cause?
opts: Heap plus memoryOverhead exceeded the container size
The NameNode ran out of blocks
Data locality was lost
check.why: YARN counts off-heap memory too. When the total passes the container size, it kills the container, even if the heap was fine.

work: Check your Spark jobs' memoryOverhead against their container sizes.
Report files under 10 MB per table and schedule compaction.

title: Choosing to leave Hadoop

beats.say: Your boss says switch Hadoop off by December. What do you check first?

show.sub: Start with what you would lose

beats.say: The core trade is locality for elasticity. Object storage separates compute from storage, so each scales and bills on its own. You lose data locality and cheap listing, so you need table formats like Iceberg to cope.

chip.text: Pay for compute only when it runs

beats.say: The playbook: inventory tables and jobs from the metastore and YARN history. Register existing Parquet in Iceberg without copying. Dual-run, reconcile counts, then switch consumers. Keep Hadoop if a fully used, owned cluster is cheaper, or the deadline is unrealistic.

check.q: What is the cheapest safe way to bring existing Parquet data into Iceberg?
opts: Copy everything to a new bucket first
Register the existing files in Iceberg metadata without copying
Rewrite every job in MapReduce
check.why: Zero-copy registration points Iceberg metadata at the existing files, so you avoid a costly copy and can dual-run safely.

work: Build an inventory of tables and jobs from the metastore and YARN history.
Cost a steady-load cluster against object storage plus on-demand compute.
Pick one low-risk table for a dual-run pilot.

title: The paved path

beats.say: Why can one team ship a new data pipeline in an afternoon, while another team needs a month?

Think of a new town. You could hand every family a shovel and say, build your own road. Or you could pave one good road to everywhere. A paved path is that road. It is a template project with the job skeleton, tests, checks and dashboards already in place.
The engineer only fills in the business logic. Nobody argues about folder layout or how to deploy. Everything looks the same, so anyone can help anyone.
Platform teams are judged on exactly this: how easily other engineers ship. One afternoon for a first pipeline is the goal.

check.q: What is the main purpose of a paved path?
opts: To force every team to use the same business logic
To let engineers ship a new pipeline fast by starting from a ready template
To reduce the number of engineers on the data team
check.why: A paved path removes repeated setup work like tests, CI, deployment and dashboards, so engineers only write what is unique to their pipeline.

work: Time how long your last new pipeline took from idea to first production run.
List the steps every new pipeline repeats and put them in a template repo.

title: The shared kitchen

beats.say: What happens when ten teams share one big computer cluster, and one team gets greedy?
Picture a shared office kitchen. Without rules, one team fills every burner and nobody else eats. So each team gets its own counter, called a namespace, and a limit, called a quota.
Some meals matter more, like payroll. Those get priority and go first when burners run short.
And every team gets a receipt for what it used. That is cost attribution. Now nobody can quietly burn the shared budget.

check.q: Why give each team a namespace with a quota?
opts: So one team cannot use up the whole shared cluster
So every team pays the same amount
So jobs run faster than on a dedicated cluster
check.why: Quotas cap what one team can take, which protects the others and makes usage easy to attribute.

work: Check whether every team has its own namespace and a quota.
Ask which pipelines are critical and should get higher priority.

title: Four gates on every pull request

beats.say: How do you stop a renamed column from breaking the executive dashboard at three in the morning?
Every pull request runs four gates. First, lint, which catches style and syntax mistakes in seconds. Second, unit tests on small functions, say two hundred tests in under a minute.
Third, a dry run. The job runs on a sample of fifty thousand rows, not the full ten terabytes. That catches crashes and bad joins cheaply.

Fourth, a schema check compares your output columns with the registered contract. Drop a column or change a type, and the build fails, naming the downstream owners. You pay minutes in review, not hours in production.

check.q: What does the schema check gate protect against?
opts: Slow queries on large tables
Output changes that break downstream consumers
Style mistakes in code
check.why: It compares the job's output with the registered contract, so dropped columns or changed types fail the build before consumers feel it.

work: Add a schema compatibility check to the pipeline CI.
Keep a small fixed sample dataset in the repo for dry runs.

title: Sharing a cluster without fights

beats.say: A cluster has one thousand cores and ten teams. Who gets them, and who pays?
Each team gets a Kubernetes namespace with a quota, for example two hundred cores and eight hundred gigabytes of memory. A job asking for more than the remaining quota is rejected or waits.
Priority classes decide order. Payroll gets high priority, experiments get low. If cores run short, the scheduler places important pods first, and fair scheduling shares leftovers between teams.
Every job carries a team label. Add up cores times hours per label, multiply by price, and each team sees its bill.

check.q: How is cost attributed to teams on a shared cluster?
opts: Split the total bill equally
Label every job with its team and sum resource usage per label
Give each team its own cloud account
check.why: Labels let you add up cores times hours per team and price it, which is fair and automatic.

work: Enforce a required team label with an admission rule.
Set a quota per namespace and review it every quarter.

title: Infrastructure as code and its traps

beats.say: Someone clicked a bucket into existence last spring. Nobody remembers why. Is it safe to delete?
That is why every bucket, catalog, namespace and permission lives in code, such as Terraform, and changes through pull requests. Hand-made resources have no owner, no history, and cannot be rebuilt.
Terraform keeps a state file, its memory of what it built. If someone edits a resource by hand, reality drifts from that memory, and the next apply may quietly undo the fix.
Two more traps. Two applies at once can corrupt state, so use remote state with locking. And read the plan: a renamed bucket shows as destroy then create, which can mean lost data.

check.q: A plan shows a storage bucket will be destroyed and recreated after a rename in code. What should you do?
opts: Apply it, since the plan is automatic
Stop, and move the state or protect the resource so data is not lost
Delete the state file and start again
check.why: A destroy and create deletes the data. Use a state move or lifecycle protection so the rename keeps the same resource.

work: Turn on remote state with locking and prevent_destroy on data buckets.
Run a scheduled drift check that alerts when cloud differs from code.

title: Where shared platforms break

beats.say: Why does a critical pipeline sit pending when the cluster looks half empty?
Quotas count requests, not usage. A team may request two hundred cores, use forty, and still block everyone else from the rest. Review requests against real usage and right-size them.
Priority has a price. When a critical job arrives, Kubernetes can preempt, meaning evict, lower priority pods. A long Spark job without checkpoints then loses hours of work.
Shared dashboards break when labels explode. Tagging metrics by run id makes millions of series and can crash the metrics store. Label by team, pipeline and job. Keep run ids in logs.

check.q: Why can adding a run id label to every metric hurt the metrics store?
opts: Run ids are too long to store
Each unique value creates a new time series, so series count explodes
Metrics cannot hold text
check.why: Every distinct label value makes a separate series. Unbounded values like run ids create millions and exhaust memory.

work: Compare requested and used cores per team and shrink the biggest gaps.
Add checkpointing to long jobs that run at low priority.

title: Build or buy the data platform

beats.say: Do you build your own data platform, or just pay Databricks?

Start by asking whether the capability sets you apart. Running Spark clusters rarely does. A managed service like EMR, Databricks or Confluent may cost a premium of around thirty percent, but it saves a team of four to six engineers.
Build when the premium grows larger than the team that would replace it, or when residency rules or custom needs force you. Do not build a platform for two teams.
The usual answer is the middle path. Buy the engine, build the paved path on top: templates, CI, cost attribution. That is where your rules live, and lock-in is lowest.

check.q: Two product teams need Spark pipelines. What is the best default?
opts: Build a custom scheduler and cluster manager
Use a managed service and add a thin template and CI on top
Let each team choose its own tools
check.why: At small scale the managed premium is far below a platform team's cost. A thin paved path adds consistency without the burden of running infrastructure.

work: Write a one page cost model: managed premium against engineers needed to run it yourself.
Keep the paved path tool-agnostic so you can switch engines later.

title: Proving the platform works

beats.say: Your platform shipped a year ago. How do you prove it is working?
Pick three measures. Time to first pipeline, for example from two weeks down to one afternoon. Failed runs per week per hundred pipelines. And cost per terabyte processed.
Beware gaming. Failures drop if teams stop running risky jobs, and cost drops if they stop processing. So add adoption: the share of pipelines on the paved path.
In an interview, name the metric, the baseline, the target, and what you would change if the number stalls.

check.q: Failed runs per week fell sharply. What should you check before celebrating?
opts: Whether fewer pipelines are running or adopting the platform
Whether the dashboard colors changed
Whether the quota was increased
check.why: Failures can drop because teams avoid the platform or run less. Pair reliability with adoption and volume to see real improvement.

work: Record today's baseline for time to first pipeline, failed runs and cost per terabyte.
Report adoption of the paved path next to every reliability metric.

title: The food truck behind every executor

beats.say: Why does a Spark job crawl, or simply die, when you have plenty of machines?

Picture each executor as a food truck. The whole truck is the container. Inside, the kitchen counter is the heap, where the cook does the real work. Counter space is split: some for cooking right now, some for ingredients kept for later, and a little for the cook's own tools.

Clutter builds up. Garbage collection is a cleaner who clears away dishes nobody needs. If the counter is full of things still in use, the cleaner keeps stopping the cook, and everything slows. Worse, the truck has a hard wall. Overflow the space outside the counter, and the truck gets towed.

chip.text: A full counter means constant pauses

check.q: In the food truck picture, what does a cleaner who keeps interrupting a cook stand for?
opts: Garbage collection pausing work because the heap is full of live objects
The network sending data between executors
The driver choosing how many partitions to use
check.why: Garbage collection frees unused objects. When most objects are still in use, it runs often and frees little, so tasks stall.

work: Open the Spark UI for a slow job and look at the GC time column for its tasks.
Write down the container size, heap size and overhead for one of your jobs.

title: Where your ten gigabytes really go

beats.say: You ask for a ten gigabyte executor. How much can your shuffle actually use?

show.sub: How much does a shuffle really get?

beats.say: Start with the heap, ten gigabytes. Spark reserves three hundred megabytes. Of the remaining nine point seven, sixty percent is unified memory, about five point eight gigabytes. Execution, for shuffles, joins and sorts, and storage, for cache, share that pool and borrow from each other.

The rest, about three point nine gigabytes, is user memory for your own objects and UDF data structures. Then comes overhead, outside the heap, for Python workers, native libraries and network buffers. It defaults to about ten percent, at least 384 megabytes. The container is heap plus overhead: roughly eleven gigabytes.

check.q: With a 10 GB heap and default settings, roughly how much is unified memory for execution and storage?
opts: 10 GB
About 5.8 GB
About 1 GB
check.why: Spark takes out 300 MB reserved, leaving 9.7 GB, and gives 60 percent of that, about 5.8 GB, to unified memory.

work: Calculate unified memory for your own executor size using the 300 MB and 60 percent rules.
Check what overhead your jobs get and whether the container request includes it.

title: Why the garbage collector stalls tasks

beats.say: Why does one task take ten times longer than its neighbours, with free cores sitting idle?

Garbage collection frees objects nobody references. When the heap is full of live objects, it finds little to free, so it runs again and again, and your code waits. In the Spark UI, watch for GC time above about ten percent of task time, and uneven task durations.

chip.text: GC time above 10 percent is a warning

beats.say: Three fixes. Give each task more memory by running fewer cores per executor. Create fewer objects, using built-in functions instead of UDFs, and Kryo serialisation. And give each task less data, with more partitions.

show.title: Cut GC pressure
items: Fewer cores per executor: more memory per task
More partitions: less data per task

check.q: A task shows 30 percent GC time and uneven durations. Which change targets the cause?
opts: Add more cores per executor
Replace UDFs with built-in functions and add partitions
Turn off caching on the driver
check.why: High GC means too many live objects per task. Built-ins create fewer objects and more partitions shrink the data each task holds.

work: Sort tasks by GC time in the Spark UI and flag any stage above 10 percent.
Replace one UDF with a built-in function and compare GC time.

title: Two out of memory errors, two fixes

beats.say: Two memory errors, similar words, opposite fixes. Which one is yours?

Java heap space means the heap itself filled up. Causes are a huge partition, a skewed key, or a big collect. Fix it with more partitions, skew handling, no collect on large data, or more executor memory.

OOMKilled on Kubernetes, or exceeding memory limits on YARN, means heap plus off-heap passed the container size. Python workers and Arrow buffers are common culprits. Raise memory overhead, use fewer Python UDFs, check pandas UDF batch sizes. The driver is a JVM too, so a large collect or oversized broadcast kills it.

check.q: A PySpark job is OOMKilled on Kubernetes, but the Spark heap looks healthy. What is the best first fix?
opts: Raise memory overhead
Add more shuffle partitions only
Call collect to inspect data
check.why: OOMKilled means total container memory was exceeded, often by off-heap Python or Arrow memory, which overhead covers.

work: Write a short runbook that maps each error message to its likely cause and first fix.
Audit jobs for collect calls on large results and broadcasts of big tables.

title: Do not just double the memory

beats.say: Your job runs out of memory. The cheap reflex is doubling executor size. Why is that often the wrong call?

Memory is paid for on every executor, but a skewed key overloads just one. If one partition needs eight gigabytes while the rest need one, doubling memory pays for waste across the cluster. Fix the skew or add partitions, and the job fits in a small executor.

Cores are a trade too. Fewer cores per executor gives each task more memory and less garbage collection, but you run more JVMs, each paying its own reserved memory and overhead. Bigger pods are also harder to schedule on Kubernetes. Match the fix to the error: partitions and skew for heap errors, overhead for container kills, and no large collects on the driver.

show.title: Choose by cause
items: Heap error: partitions and skew first, memory last
Container kill: raise overhead, cut Python UDFs
Fewer cores: less GC, but more JVM overhead
Driver: no big collect, broadcast only small tables

check.q: One skewed key causes a heap OutOfMemoryError on a single task. What is the most cost-effective fix?
opts: Double memory on every executor
Fix the skew or split the hot key
Raise memory overhead
check.why: Only one partition is oversized. Fixing the skew removes the cause, whereas bigger executors make every node pay for one hot key.

work: Before raising memory on a failing job, check the stage's max versus median task size to spot skew.
Compare cost for fewer cores per executor against the extra JVM overhead on one job.
Set a team rule that large results are written to storage, not collected to the driver.
